name: Battles of Lexington and Concord

phases.title: The militia stand on Lexington Common
phases.text: About 80 Lexington militiamen formed up on the Common in plain sight, but not across the road to Concord. Pitcairn's advance guard entered Lexington, with Smith's remaining companies further down the road.

phases.title: The Regulars charge and the militia disperse
phases.text: After shots were fired, of which the accounts disagree on the first, the Regulars charged with bayonets. Eight Lexington men were killed and ten wounded, and the militia fell back.

phases.title: The Concord militia withdraw to a hill north of the bridge
phases.text: The militia of Acton, Concord and Lincoln marched out to meet the Regulars, then turned back, as the Regulars numbered about 700 and they about 250. Barrett led them across the Old North Bridge to a hill about a mile north.

phases.title: The Regulars search Concord
phases.text: Smith reformed the column and marched to Concord, where he divided it to search for supplies. Four companies under Captain Parsons went beyond the North Bridge, while Laurie's companies guarded it. Barrett's militia watched from a hill to the north.

phases.title: The militia advance and the British fall back to the bridge
phases.text: Seeing only a few light infantry companies below, Barrett marched his men down to a flat hilltop about 300 yards from the Old North Bridge. The two British companies holding the position near the road retreated to the bridge.

phases.title: The fight at the North Bridge
phases.text: Barrett's militia advanced on the bridge and exchanged fire with Laurie's companies, who broke and fled to the grenadiers coming from the town. This isolated the four companies at the farm.

phases.title: The rear guard fires at Meriam's Corner
phases.text: Parsons' companies came back to the town and the Regulars left Concord after noon. At Meriam's Corner the rear guard wheeled and fired a volley at militia who had closed to musket range, and the militia returned fire with deadly effect.

phases.title: The Regulars charge Brooks Hill
phases.text: Beyond Meriam's Corner the leading Regulars charged up Brooks Hill, where nearly 500 militiamen had gathered. The colonists did not withdraw and inflicted heavy casualties on the attackers, and Smith drew his men back from the hill.

phases.title: Crossfire at the Bloody Angle
phases.text: At a sharp bend where the road curved left, militia caught the British in a crossfire from both sides, and again at a second bend further on. The British lost thirty killed or wounded and escaped by breaking into a trot.

phases.title: Parker's militia ambush the column near Lexington
phases.text: Near the boundary between Lincoln and Lexington, Parker's men, some of them bandaged, ambushed the column from a hill overlooking the road. Smith was wounded in the thigh and Pitcairn sent light infantry up the hill to clear the militia.

phases.title: Percy's brigade arrives and its guns open fire
phases.text: A brigade of about 1,000 men with artillery under Earl Percy arrived at about 2:30 pm. Percy ordered his guns to fire at extreme range, which dispersed the pursuing militia, and Smith's men collapsed with exhaustion when they reached his lines.

phases.title: Fighting through Menotomy at Jason Russell's farm
phases.text: The column left Lexington with flankers on both sides and a rear guard rotated every mile or so. Fighting grew more intense in Menotomy, where hundreds of militiamen had gathered at Jason Russell's farm.

phases.title: Percy turns onto the Charlestown road
phases.text: At Watson's Corner Percy used his two guns and flankers on fresh militia. He then led his troops down a narrow track onto the road to Charlestown. The militia, about 4,000, were unprepared for it, and the circle of fire was broken.

note: The plan shows the whole running fight along the road from Lexington to Concord and back to Charlestown, not a single field. Distances are only roughly to scale, and the accounts do not say which side of the road each hill and farm lay on; those are placed by judgement. The accounts differ on who fired the first shot at Lexington; the plan does not decide it.
